explanation:
The functions `pthread_attr_setschedpolicy` and `pthread_attr_getschedpolicy` are core components of the POSIX threads (pthreads) library, designed to manage the scheduling policy attribute within a thread attributes object (`pthread_attr_t`). This attribute determines how the operating system kernel will allocate CPU time to any thread subsequently created using this attributes object.

The `pthread_attr_setschedpolicy` function is used to assign a specific scheduling policy. It requires two parameters: a pointer to the thread attributes object (`pthread_attr_t *attr`) and an integer `policy`. Standard supported policies include `SCHED_FIFO` (First-In, First-Out real-time scheduling), `SCHED_RR` (Round-Robin real-time scheduling), and `SCHED_OTHER` (the default, time-sharing policy). Using real-time policies (`SCHED_FIFO` or `SCHED_RR`) usually requires the calling process to possess elevated privileges (such as the `CAP_SYS_NICE` capability under Linux) to prevent unauthorized resource exhaustion.

Conversely, `pthread_attr_getschedpolicy` retrieves the currently configured scheduling policy from the attributes object specified by `attr` and writes the resulting integer value into the memory location pointed to by `policy`. This allows verification of the attribute settings.

Both functions return 0 upon successful execution. In the event of an error, they return a non-zero error number, often corresponding to POSIX error codes. A common error for `pthread_attr_setschedpolicy` is `EINVAL`, indicating that the value passed in `policy` is not a valid or recognized scheduling discipline. POSIX also notes that some implementations may return `ENOTSUP` if the requested policy is not supported by the underlying system architecture.

It is vital to note the interaction with scheduling inheritance. For the policy set via `pthread_attr_setschedpolicy` to actually govern a new thread's behavior, the programmer must ensure that the thread attributes object's inheritance flag is set to `PTHREAD_EXPLICIT_SCHED` using the `pthread_attr_setinheritsched(3)` function. If inheritance is left at the default setting (`PTHREAD_INHERIT_SCHED`), the new thread will simply adopt the scheduling policy of the parent thread, ignoring the explicit policy setting in the attributes object.
keywords: pthread_attr_setschedpolicy, pthread_attr_getschedpolicy, SCHED_FIFO, SCHED_RR, SCHED_OTHER, scheduling policy, thread attributes, pthread_attr_t, PTHREAD_EXPLICIT_SCHED, real-time scheduling, pthreads
example_explanation: This code initializes a thread attributes object, attempts to set the scheduling policy to SCHED_RR, ensures the inheritance flag is set to PTHREAD_EXPLICIT_SCHED, and finally uses `pthread_attr_getschedpolicy` to confirm the policy value stored within the attribute object.
